articles.title: Building arkiv: a CLI for a database that lives on a blockchain
articles.excerpt: Arkiv lets you write entities to a chain and query them by attribute, like a database where every row is signed and expires on a schedule. The SDK is solid. The docs are decent. What was missing was t…
articles.body: Arkiv lets you write entities to a chain and query them by attribute, like a database where every row is signed and expires on a schedule. The SDK is solid. The docs are decent. What was missing was the ten minutes before any of that matters: checking that your machine can talk to the network, that your key actually works, that the schema you are about to invent has not already been invented by three other people this week. So I built arkiv , a terminal toolkit for the network. Nine commands, two runtime dependencies, and a test suite that runs against the built output. This post is about the decisions inside it, including the three bugs that only showed up when I took screenshots of real runs.

articles.title: When the agent writes the patch, who audits the tests?
articles.excerpt: In the METR randomized trial published in July 2025, sixteen experienced open-source developers worked on 246 real issues in their own repositories. Half the tasks allowed AI tools, half did not. The…
articles.body: In the METR randomized trial published in July 2025, sixteen experienced open-source developers worked on 246 real issues in their own repositories. Half the tasks allowed AI tools, half did not. The AI-allowed tasks took 19% longer. Before the study the same developers expected a 24% speedup, and after living through the slowdown they still believed they had been sped up by 20%. That gap between what happened and what the developers felt is the most useful result in the paper, and it is not really about coding speed. It is about measurement. People are bad at knowing whether a tool helped, and the tool is now producing the thing that tells them. Apply that to tests and you get the quiet failure nobody is writing postmortems about yet. The agent writes the code.

articles.title: Laravel Sanctum vs Passport vs JWT: Which Auth to Use
articles.excerpt: "Sanctum, Passport or JWT?" gets asked as if the three were competitors. They aren't quite. Sanctum and Passport are first-party Laravel packages. JWT is not a package at all: it's a token format (RFC…
articles.body: "Sanctum, Passport or JWT?" gets asked as if the three were competitors. They aren't quite. Sanctum and Passport are first-party Laravel packages. JWT is not a package at all: it's a token format (RFC 7519) that third-party Laravel packages build on. The useful question is not "which is best" but who is calling your API, and do you need OAuth2? For most Laravel applications the answer is Sanctum, and Laravel's own documentation says so. This article explains why, shows what each option does with real output, and covers the cases where Passport or JWT is the right call. I ran Sanctum 4.4.0 in a Laravel 13.40 app and tested JWT behavior with firebase/php-jwt 7.2.1. Passport I could only check against the documentation, and I say so where it matters.

articles.title: Realtime Channel Teardown: Idempotent Recovery for Multiplayer Quiz Sessions
articles.excerpt: Short answer: treat channel deletion as a recorded state transition, not as a socket operation, and make every reconnect replay the same ordered event log. That decision keeps a multiplayer quiz game…
articles.body: Short answer: treat channel deletion as a recorded state transition, not as a socket operation, and make every reconnect replay the same ordered event log. That decision keeps a multiplayer quiz game correct when a host closes a room while answers, timers, and reconnect requests are still in flight. I build payment and ledger backends, so I am suspicious of the phrase “delete the room.” Deletion sounds like one write, but it actually crosses the room registry, presence state, answer submissions, timer workers, and the audit trail. A player can receive a final question after the host has ended the game; a reconnect can arrive after the delete request but before its broadcast; a retry can execute the same command twice. The failure is not cosmetic. It can change a score.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.

SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off.
